title: Yitzchak Resh Galuta
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: In Yevamot 115b (cited by Hyman as קמו:), he was Rav Bibi’s sister’s son. He was traveling from Kurtaba to Aspamya and died. Word was sent from there of his death. The Gemara asks whether there might be a second Yitzchak Resh Galuta. Hyman reports that Seder HaDorot cites the Rosh’s responsa, klal 50, for the view that this was his name and that he did not hold the office of Exilarch. The argument is that one would hardly raise a doubt about a second Yitzchak Resh Galuta if this were the Exilarch known throughout the Diaspora.

notes.text: The supplied locator קמו: means 146b, beyond Yevamot’s folio range. The matching passage is 115b. Kurtaba and Aspamya are retained as names without asserting that they are modern Cordoba and Spain. The Rosh’s view that Resh Galuta was a name rather than an office remains attributed.

No new primary scalar was returned. The earlier recorded Yevamot match is 115b beside supplied קמו:, conventionally146b, which is outside the tractate’s range; the older119b guess is not adopted. Kurtaba and Aspamya remain names without modern geographic identification. The source says Rav Bibi’s SISTER’S SON. The Rosh, responsa klal50, via Seder HaDorot argues that Resh Galuta was his name rather than the Exilarch office; this remains attributed reasoning. Supplied ישלחו is read narratively as they sent, without changing its letters. No office-holder identity is admitted.

Hyman’s print (vol. II, p. 803) gives קמו: (146b). Seder HaDorot itself cites Yevamot 115b and attributes the byname argument to the Rosh, klal 50. In the consulted Teshuvot HaRosh 51:2, the reply addressed to “my father” argues that Resh Galuta was a byname or family name, while the opening letter assumes Yitzchak held the office. The two positions belong to different voices within the responsum.
